PullRequest.Title: chat: add opt-in persistent working progress
PullRequest.Body:
## Summary

Adds an opt-in persistent working indicator with the VS Code logo, plus selectable logo animations and component-explorer coverage.

### Settings

Both settings are off by default:

```json
"chat.experimental.persistentProgress.enabled": false,
"chat.experimental.persistentProgress.animation": "off"
```

Enable persistent progress separately from choosing an animation. The animation choices are **Off** (static logo), **Weave**, **Orbit and Lock**, **Accordion**, and **Dial Rotation**. Changes update existing indicators immediately. Reduced motion disables logo animation.

### Progress behavior

- Keep the working indicator at the end of an active response until completion or cancellation, including while tools stream, terminals produce output, subagents finish, and interactive prompts are shown.
- Preserve the **collapsed-thinking exception**: while the last active thinking section owns progress, its logo stays in the header; the header prefix shimmers when collapsed and the inner working label shimmers when expanded. Fixed Scrolling and Collapsed Preview keep the response footer instead and omit the inner working row.
- Preserve the original progress UI when the setting is disabled. Terminal activity animations and the new rich subagent pills remain unchanged.
- Replace redundant pending plan-review progress with the persistent indicator while retaining the review widget and completed summary.
- Refresh question, plan-review, elicitation, and authentication status immediately after interaction, without waiting for more provider output.
- Retain the footer DOM and logo animation across streaming updates and subagent completion notices. Refresh working phrases on logical activity changes with a minimum dwell time, not on every token.

### Logo and fixtures

- Use the same three-piece Stable silhouette for both Stable blue and Insiders green tints, with theme colors and high-contrast support.
- Animate fixed SVG faces through HTML-wrapper transforms and opacity; no animation-frame JavaScript or path morphing.
- Include in-chat scenario groups for all three thinking styles, the supported animation settings, terminal commands/output/approvals, questions, confirmations, plan reviews, worktree creation, MCP startup, and classic/rich parallel subagents.
- Retain the explored motion designs and Weave V comparison in the component explorer. Tests cover geometry, independent ribbon paths, loop seams, reduced motion, and disposal.

### Toolbar rollback

Also removes the three picker-label `translateY(1px)` offsets introduced in `6230521f531d4a9daab79dac0dc2c53e3b967710`, as requested during iteration. Picker functionality and newer spacing changes are preserved; this does not introduce a toolbar redesign.

## Validation

After merging latest `main` (`3e8601c5f63`):

- `npm run gulp compile-client` — passed with zero errors.
- Repository hygiene across the final PR diff — passed.
- 12 affected chat/configuration/logo/picker/terminal test suites — **466 passing, 1 existing pending test**.
- `git diff --check` — passed.

Earlier live-browser validation covered Dark/Light thinking styles, interaction completion without provider updates, stable progress through terminal output and subagent notices, restored terminal animation, and unchanged rich subagent pills. Isolated 16px logo traces recorded no steady-state Layout/Paint events in four-second samples; that measurement excludes text shimmer and GPU work.

The feature commit and main merge are both GPG-signed. No signing or verification hooks were bypassed.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The reachable production enum and repository-wide references establish that these animation definitions are fixture-only, and the static production CSS import establishes the eager load. The exact startup milliseconds are uncertain, hence low severity.
Findings.PerformanceResource: Production CSS bytes, parsed selectors/keyframes, and stylesheet memory
Findings.PerformanceScaling: This fixed cost is paid whenever the Chat renderer stylesheet is loaded, for every window/session, regardless of whether persistent progress is enabled; roughly twenty unused motion families account for most of the new 612-line stylesheet.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Increased Chat/workbench load and stylesheet parsing cost plus retained style data for animations users cannot select.
Findings.PreviousBehavior: The production bundle had no chat-working-logo stylesheet or prototype motion definitions.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: The new production stylesheet includes Weave V and roughly twenty other explored animation families, while production configuration exposes only Weave, Orbit, Accordion, and Dial. Repository references show the extra `ChatWorkingLogoMotion` values are used only by the component fixture and tests, yet `chatWorkingLogo.ts` statically imports this entire CSS file.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: RIGHT line 102 starts an added animation family that is unreachable from production configuration but is nevertheless included in the newly imported production stylesheet.
Findings.Title: Keep component-explorer animations out of the production stylesheet
Findings.Impact: Users load and parse most of a ~24 KB stylesheet even when the opt-in feature is disabled, and those extra keyframes can never be reached through product settings.
Findings.Evidence: The first non-product family begins at line 102 (`weave-v`) and the file continues through 612 lines with fold, relay, stack, shutter, aperture, magnet, trace, pendulum, prism, ladder, carousel, piston, bridge, fan, comb, braid, sling, folio, and helix. `ChatProgressAnimation` exposes only off/weave/orbit/accordion/dial, while repository search finds the remaining motions only in `chatWorkingLogo.fixture.ts` and tests. `chatWorkingLogo.ts:13` imports the CSS from production code.
Findings.Recommendation: Move exploratory motion classes/keyframes and their duration/type entries into component-fixture-only files; keep the production module and stylesheet limited to the four selectable animations.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The call path from the added argument to the infinite background-position animation is explicit, and every persistent state is explicitly active. Exact device-level cost is hardware-dependent, so severity is low, but the continuous paint mechanism and response-lifetime trigger are deterministic.
Findings.PerformanceResource: Continuous CSS background-position painting for the persistent progress label
Findings.PerformanceScaling: The paint work runs continuously for the full lifetime of every enabled in-progress response, including long tool runs and indefinitely blocked question, confirmation, plan-review, and authentication states; it also multiplies across concurrently visible chat windows.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Sustained renderer CPU/GPU usage and battery drain, with avoidable frame contention during long responses.
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Before this feature, a footer shimmer was conditional and absent while normal markdown streamed or specialized tool/interaction UI owned progress; there was no response-lifetime text animation.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: This argument forces `useShimmer` on for every persistent working part. The existing `.shimmer-progress` rule animates `background-position` every two seconds forever, and all persistent states are emitted with `isActive: true`, even when waiting for user input. The separate progress-animation setting only makes the logo static and does not stop this text animation.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: RIGHT line 383 newly passes `isActive` as the shimmer flag for every persistent working row; the PR also newly creates that row throughout the response rather than only at legacy progress pauses.
Findings.Title: Stop repainting the progress text for the entire response
Findings.Impact: With `chat.experimental.persistentProgress.enabled` on (even with its default animation value `off`), every response continuously repaints the progress label until completion. Long-running agents or prompts left awaiting input therefore keep the renderer doing frame work while otherwise idle.
Findings.Evidence: The added constructor argument at line 383 makes persistent progress shimmer whenever `isActive` is true. `getPersistentWorkingProgress` sets `isActive: true` for active, question, confirmation, plan review, and authentication states (chatListRenderer.ts:1985-2009). `chat.css:3465-3478` applies `animation: chat-thinking-shimmer 2s linear infinite` and `will-change: background-position`; its keyframes at chat.css:192-199 mutate background-position, a paint-triggering property. Reduced motion is the only rule that disables it.
Findings.Recommendation: Keep the persistent label but avoid a response-lifetime background-position animation: make the text static while output is streaming or the response is user-blocked, or implement the shimmer with a bounded/compositor-friendly transform and stop it after a short cycle.

Scenarios.Scenario: Normal response streaming with persistent progress enabled
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Each model update reaches ChatListItemRenderer's incremental/progressive render path, retains or updates one footer, and leaves its text shimmer active until completion. Rendering is on the UI critical path; no subprocess, IPC, filesystem, database, or network call is added by the diff.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: One progress footer per active visible response; update work scales with streamed response-part count and update frequency, while the reported CSS paint scales with total response duration and concurrently visible active chat windows.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Rendering remains serialized on the renderer/UI thread. Typically one response per widget is actively streaming, with possible multiplication across windows/widgets; there is no new limiter or asynchronous fan-out.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The footer DOM and logo are intentionally retained across updates, and a WeakMap keeps one phrase record per live response. There is no I/O cache. Warm renders reuse the footer; cold render creates three SVG faces once.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the persistent constructor forces shimmer, all persistent states are active, and the CSS animates background-position infinitely.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The painted text area is small and hardware/compositor behavior varies, so exact CPU, battery, and frame impact is uncertain; this is reflected in low severity.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable low-severity rendering regression because an opt-in persistent row now performs paint-triggering animation for the complete response lifetime, including periods where previous footer progress was absent.

Scenarios.Scenario: Responses blocked on questions, confirmations, plan review, authentication, or MCP startup
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The response waits on user interaction or pre-existing MCP work. Added callbacks refresh the footer after interaction/state completion; those UI refreshes do not initiate the external work and are off the external operation's critical path. While blocked, the persistent text animation remains active and continues rendering work.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Existing MCP server startup and authentication represented to these content parts through status observables
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: The UI renders one grouped status part for the server collection and invokes one completion refresh when startup/authentication finishes; it does not add per-server boundary calls.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same MCP startup/authentication occurred before the diff; the PR only suppresses a competing spinner and refreshes the persistent footer.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The external MCP work gates provider progress, while the changed UI callbacks merely update status after that work and do not add latency to the operation itself.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One interaction widget/footer per blocked response; confirmation refresh callbacks can scale with confirmation count, but observed updates are bounded by interaction transitions and did not justify a separate finding. Animation cost scales with how long prompts are left unanswered.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Interaction callbacks are queued as microtasks and UI rendering is serialized. Parallel subagent confirmations can enqueue multiple callbacks, but state checks and content deduplication bound most duplicate DOM mutation.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No response-state cache is introduced. Existing DOM parts are diffed/reused; phrase state uses weak keys. MCP server/status observables retain their existing lifecycle.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High for the continuous blocked-state animation; high that no new external boundary is invoked by the changed UI code.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Prompt dwell time ranges from seconds to hours, and the per-frame cost varies by display and hardware.
Scenarios.Verdict: The indefinite blocked-state portion strengthens the reported continuous-paint finding. The MCP/interaction callbacks themselves do not establish a separate boundary or fan-out regression.

Scenarios.Scenario: Chat UI/style initialization and progress animation selection
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Loading the production ChatWorkingLogo module statically loads and parses its stylesheet before any logo can render. Configuration changes update existing logo classes synchronously but perform no I/O.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: The stylesheet cost is fixed per loaded workbench/window, independent of response count; active configuration listeners scale with the small number of live progress logos.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: CSS parsing/style registration occurs in the renderer's normal load sequence. Logo configuration updates fan out synchronously to live logo instances, normally one footer and at most one thinking-header owner.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Built resources may be cached on disk between launches, but each renderer still parses/registers the stylesheet. There is no conditional cache keyed on the opt-in setting; disabled and enabled users load the same rules.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: production exposes four motions, repository references place the other motions only in fixtures/tests, and the production module statically imports all 612 lines.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Build minification and platform stylesheet loading affect exact byte and startup-time cost, so severity is low.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable low-severity eager-work regression because most newly shipped animation CSS is unreachable from production and can be isolated to component fixtures.

Scenarios.Scenario: Toggling persistent progress and animation settings
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Changing the enabled setting refreshes the chat list once so existing rows switch presentation; changing only the animation updates live logos through per-logo configuration listeners without rerendering response content.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: The enabled-setting refresh scales with visible/list-rendered chat items. Animation-setting updates scale with live logo instances, not chat history.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Both paths are synchronous UI updates with the list refresh serialized by the widget; no background concurrency or boundary fan-out is introduced.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Existing parts are cleared when presentation mode changes and rebuilt once; subsequent streaming reuses the new footer. No external caches or negative-cache behavior apply.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High based on ChatListWidget's configuration listener and ChatWorkingProgressLogo's listener/disposal ownership.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Visible history size varies, but setting changes are infrequent and user initiated.
Scenarios.Verdict: No additional reportable regression: the one-time list refresh is necessary to apply the setting, and logo listeners are disposed with their content parts.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all 40 changed files and relevant renderer/content-part call paths. Reported the persistent text's response-lifetime paint animation and fixture-only motion CSS shipped eagerly; inspected rendering reuse, configuration refresh, interaction/MCP callbacks, disposal, cache behavior, and boundary/concurrency behavior without finding another high-confidence regression.
